extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (and self-learners) studying linear algebra; readers of Evan Chen's Napkin notes
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and records linear-algebra definitions, constructions, and criteria for eigen-things, tensor/wedge products, trace and determinant, dual space, and inner products as presented in a textbook-style exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jordan-chain basis construction (basis B of generalized eigenvectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct B as concatenation of Jordan 'staircases' v_i, T(v_i), T(T(v_i)), ... for i = 1..ℓ, followed by additional vectors v_{ℓ+1},...,v_m forming a basis for ker T. Check there are exactly ℓ + dim W + (dim ker T − ℓ) = dim V elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: exactly ℓ elements of the preliminary set B' lie in ker T (the last element of each staircase); complete those to a basis of ker T by adding m−ℓ vectors (where m = dim ker T). Exercise 10.7.2: show all elements are linearly independent (hint in text: assume a dependence and apply T to reach contradiction). This construction yields a basis of the desired form (a Jordan-chain/generalized eigenvector basis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric multiplicity (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The geometric multiplicity of λ is the dimension dim V_λ of the λ-eigenspace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently (Proposition 10.8.4) the geometric multiplicity equals the number of Jordan blocks with eigenvalue λ; the eigenspace has one basis element per Jordan block. Example: for a given Jordan-form matrix with eigenvalue 7, the eigenspace had basis e1 and e4 so geometric multiplicity = 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic multiplicity (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The algebraic multiplicity of λ is the dimension dim V^λ of the generalized eigenspace (the subspace of v with (T−λ id)^n(v)=0 for some n≥1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice one counts Jordan blocks: the algebraic multiplicity is the sum of the sizes (dimensions) of the Jordan blocks with eigenvalue λ. Example: in the running example with λ=7, the generalized eigenspace had basis e1,e2,e4,e5,e6 so algebraic multiplicity = 5. (Silly edge case: multiplicity zero if λ is not an eigenvalue.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation: geometric ≤ algebraic multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric multiplicity is always less than or equal to algebraic multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 10.8.5 asks to show dim eigenspace ≤ dim generalized eigenspace; follows from Jordan block structure since each Jordan block contributes exactly one eigenvector but possibly multiple generalized eigenvectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonalizability criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear map T is diagonalizable if it has a basis consisting entirely of eigenvectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over an algebraically closed field, T is diagonalizable iff for every eigenvalue λ the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity (Problem 10B). Interpretational note: 'diagonalizable' refers to representation by a diagonal matrix in some basis (hence name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product V ⊗ W (definition and basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: V ⊗_k W is the vector space generated by pure tensors v ⊗ w subject to bilinearity relations: (v1+v2)⊗w = v1⊗w+v2⊗w, v⊗(w1+w2)=v⊗w1+v⊗w2, (c·v)⊗w = v⊗(c·w).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure tensors generate V⊗W (but most elements are sums of pure tensors). If e1..em is a basis of V and f1..fn a basis of W then {ei⊗fj} is a basis of V⊗W and dim(V⊗W)=dim V · dim W. Examples: R[x]⊗R[y] = R[x,y]. Warning (Remark 11.1.3/11.1.7): not every element is a single pure tensor; scalars 'float' across the ⊗ wall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual space V^∨ and dual basis
rubrics_metrics.description: V^∨ is the vector space of linear maps V → k. Given basis e1..en of V, define dual basis e^∨_i by e^∨_i(e_j)=1 if i=j, else 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: elements of V^∨ act like row vectors evaluating column vectors. Proposition 11.2.3: e^∨_1,...,e^∨_n is a basis of V^∨. The isomorphism V ≅ V^∨ given by choosing a basis is basis-dependent (unnatural); Example remark shows different bases give different identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hom(V,W) ≅ V^∨ ⊗ W (representation of linear maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural isomorphism Ψ : V^∨ ⊗ W → Hom(V,W) sending ξ1⊗w1 + ... + ξm⊗wm to the linear map v ↦ Σ ξ_i(v) w_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surjectivity construction: for T with T(ei)=wi, the element Σ e^∨_i ⊗ wi maps to T. Dimension argument (dim V^∨ ⊗ W = dim V · dim W = dim Hom(V,W)) shows Ψ is an isomorphism. Example 11.3.4 exhibits the correspondence for a 2×2 matrix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace (coordinate-free definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace Tr T is the evaluation of Hom(V,V) ≅ V^∨ ⊗ V under ev : V^∨ ⊗ V → k given by f⊗v ↦ f(v); i.e., Tr is the composition Hom(V,V) ≅ V^∨⊗V →_ev k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This coordinate-free definition implies the usual diagonal-sum formula in coordinates. Alternative/equivalent notion (when eigenvalues exist): Tr T is the sum of eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity (Problem 11A). Example 11.4.1: compute Tr of a 2×2 matrix as 1+4=5. Related problems: Tr(T⊗S)=Tr(T)·Tr(S) (Problem 11B†), Tr(T◦S)=Tr(S◦T) (Problem 11C†).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedge product Vm(V) and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Vm(V) is generated by wedges v1∧...∧vm subject to multilinearity and relations v∧v=0 (hence antisymmetry v∧w = −w∧v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basis for Vm(V): {e_{i1}∧...∧e_{im} | 1≤i1<...<im≤n}, so dim Vm(V)=C(n,m). Interpretation: wedge encodes oriented volumes (e.g., v∧w in R^2 gives area ad−bc). The wedge construction is used to define the determinant via top wedge space V^n(V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant (wedge/top-form definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n-dimensional V, the induced map V^n(T) : V^n(V) → V^n(V) is multiplication by a scalar; that scalar is det T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because V^n(V) is one-dimensional, V^n(T) corresponds to multiplication by det T. Consequences: det(S◦T)=det S · det T, Leibniz formula arises by expanding wedges, and for 2×2 matrices det = ad−bc (Example 12.2.3). Problem 12B: det T equals the product of eigenvalues (counted with algebraic multiplicity). Determinant nonzero ⇔ T is an isomorphism (Problem 12D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic polynomial and Cayley–Hamilton
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristic polynomial p_T(X) can be defined as det(X·id − T) and equals ∏_{i=1}^n (X−λ_i) when eigenvalues λ_i exist; Cayley–Hamilton: p_T(T)=0 (the zero map).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cayley–Hamilton proof via Jordan decomposition: if V = ⊕ J_i with Ji a Jordan block of size d_i and eigenvalue λ_i, then p_T(T) factors as Π (T−λ_i)^{d_i} which vanishes on each Ji. Example 12.3.2 verifies for a 2×2 matrix. Remark: characteristic polynomial can be defined without mentioning eigenvalues; tensoring/complexification arguments extend results beyond algebraically closed fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of algebraic multiplicities equals dim V
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of algebraic multiplicities of all eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) equals dim V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 10A frames this: given an n-dimensional vector space, the sum of algebraic multiplicities over all eigenvalues is n. This follows from counting sizes of all Jordan blocks (algebraic multiplicities partition the dimension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real inner product (definition and properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A real inner form ⟨·,·⟩ : V×V → R is symmetric, bilinear (linear in each argument), and positive definite (⟨v,v⟩ ≥ 0 with equality only for v=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation ⟨v,w⟩ generalizes the dot product in R^n; properties yield notions of orthogonality (⟨v,w⟩=0) and norm |v|^2=⟨v,v⟩. Exercise 13.1.2: show linearity in one argument plus symmetry implies linearity in the other.
